name: Sloop 28

places.name: Cockpit
places.description: You're in the cockpit, teak-slatted seats worn pale, the tiller beside you and the key panel on the bulkhead.

places.name: Companionway
places.description: You're in the companionway hatch, a hand on the cold grab rail, the saloon below and the quarter berth at your knee.

places.name: Quarter berth
places.description: You're in the quarter berth, knees on the cushion, the engine panel by your shoulder.

places.name: Saloon
places.description: You're in the saloon, the table folded, the air cool and a little damp.

places.name: Forepeak
places.description: You're in the forepeak, bent under the deck hatch, sail bags and a coil of old anchor warp around your feet.

places.name: On deck
places.description: You're up on deck, the mast stepped in the middle, dew on the cabin top and the whole yard laid out below.

places.name: Beside the hull
places.description: You're on the gravel beside the hull, her keel at head height and the cradle pads around you.
places.way: down the ladder to the ground beside the hull

covers.name: Companionway steps
covers.removeText: You lift the steps out and stand them against the bulkhead; the front of the engine looks up at you.
covers.refitText: You slot the steps back into their runners and they sit square.

covers.name: Quarter-berth panel
covers.removeText: Two screws, a tug on the plywood, and the side of the engine is open to you.
covers.refitText: You hold the panel up to its frame and run the two screws home.

covers.name: Battery-box lid
covers.removeText: You unhook the lid and fold it back on its pin; the smell of acid comes up with the cold.
covers.refitText: You fold the lid down and hook it shut.

covers.name: Cockpit-locker lid
covers.removeText: You lift the seat lid and prop it open; fenders, a tin of rags, and the tank down below.
covers.refitText: You lower the seat lid and sit on it to be sure.

covers.name: Saloon floorboards
covers.removeText: You lift the floorboards one by one and stack them on the settee; the bilge smells of brine.
covers.refitText: You lay the floorboards back in their order, shoulder to shoulder.

covers.name: Companionway hatch
covers.refitText: You slide the hatch shut and drop in the washboard.

covers.name: Bilge pump fuse
covers.removeText: You pull the bilge pump fuse out of its holder.
covers.refitText: You push the bilge pump fuse back into its holder.
covers.refitLog: Put the bilge pump fuse back in.

positions.label: Below the companionway, above the engine

components.name: Start battery
components.description: A black 70 Ah lead-acid battery, case dusty, date stamped three summers back. The vents are dry.

atSea.text: The battery is low; it may not turn the engine over again once you stop it.

faults.name: Battery at 60 % charge

reveals.text: Resting voltage says about 60 %.

faults.consequence: Slow cranking, and a flat battery after a few starts.

yard.how: The yard fits a new battery

faults.name: Battery soaked in bilge water

reveals.text: A tide line of bilge scum on the battery case, the terminals furred green underneath.

faults.consequence: The battery leaks its charge away and will not hold it for long.

yard.how: The yard fits a new battery

atSea.text: The battery is dead; nothing will start the engine, and the bilge pump has nothing to run on.

faults.name: Frozen, dead battery

spawn.cause: The battery has frozen and split. It came on after {n} night{s} of frost with the battery flat and left aboard.

reveals.text: The meter reads next to nothing at rest, and under the starter it collapses to nothing at all.
The case is swollen at the sides and a crack weeps along one seam: the frost has had the electrolyte.

faults.consequence: She will not start, and the bilge pump has nothing to run on.

yard.how: The yard fits a new battery

faults.note: UNVERIFIED (design note 008): that a flat lead-acid battery freezes and splits after a couple of frosty nights is a domain claim not yet checked with Amit.

components.name: Battery switch
components.description: A red-knobbed rotary switch, knob faded pink where the light from the hatch falls on it. It turns with a gritty click.

components.name: Positive terminal
components.description: A lead clamp under a red rubber boot, bolt snug.

removablePart.name: rubber boot
removablePart.uncoveredText: Dull grey lead, a trace of white bloom at the edge of the clamp, the bolt snug.

faults.name: Strained positive terminal

reveals.text: The clamp is discoloured with heat, bluish at the edge, and the lug is bent from the long drags on the starter.
The meter shows a real drop across the clamp while she cranks: it is eating volts.

faults.consequence: The starter gets less and less each time; one day it only clicks.

diy.how: Clean the clamp and straighten the lug, or fit a new terminal

yard.how: The yard fits a new terminal and lug

components.name: Main positive cable
components.description: A fat red cable, sleeve stiff with age but unbroken. It runs forward along the box wall.

removablePart.name: rubber boot
removablePart.uncoveredText: Dull grey lug, a trace of white bloom where it meets the cable, the nut snug.

components.name: Negative terminal
components.description: A lead clamp under a black rubber boot, greasy from some earlier owner's smear of vaseline.

removablePart.name: rubber boot
removablePart.uncoveredText: Dull grey lead, a trace of white bloom at the edge of the clamp, the bolt snug.

faults.name: Corroded negative terminal

reveals.text: Dull grey lead, white bloom along the edge of the clamp, the bolt snug.
That's far too much voltage lost across one clamp.
You pull the clamp off and find a ring of green-white crust on the post, eating into the lead.

faults.consequence: The engine won't start.

diy.how: Clean the post and clamp, and tighten it

yard.how: The yard electrician cleans and re-terminates the battery cables

components.name: Negative cable
components.description: A black cable of the same gauge as its red twin, a little greener at the lugs.

removablePart.name: rubber boot
removablePart.uncoveredText: Dull grey lug, a trace of white bloom where it meets the cable, the nut snug.

components.name: Engine ground stud
components.description: A brass stud on the engine foot with a ring lug and a nut. Dull, but it holds.

removablePart.name: rubber cap
removablePart.uncoveredText: Dull brass, a trace of bloom where the lug meets the stud, the nut snug.

faults.name: Engine ground stud soaked in bilge water

reveals.text: The ground stud wears a crust of bilge scum, the ring lug green and the nut rusted fast.

faults.consequence: The ground connection resists the starter's current and the engine cranks slowly.

diy.how: Clean and tighten the stud, or fit a new one

yard.how: The yard cleans the ground stud

components.name: Starter solenoid
components.description: A small silver can bolted on top of the starter. Paint blistered; it clicks when called.

components.name: Starter motor
components.description: A heavy cylinder on the flywheel housing, caked with old oil and a fine grey dust. Smells of warm copper.
components.note: seriesOhms 0.045 is an unverified placeholder, decision 2

faults.name: Starter soaked in bilge water

reveals.text: A tide line of bilge scum on the starter body, rust blooming at the bolts.

faults.consequence: The starter cranks slower as the corrosion works in, and one day it will not turn.

yard.how: The yard fits a new starter motor

components.name: Ignition panel
components.description: A cockpit panel with a key, two warning lamps and a tachometer that has read 800 for years. The plastic has clouded.

components.name: Fuel tank
components.description: A grey aluminium tank under the cockpit sole, tidy welds, a little white bloom at the bottom seam.

atSea.text: When the sea gets up, the engine may cough and die.

faults.name: Water in the fuel tank

reveals.text: Under the diesel a clear line of water sits in the bottom of the bowl, two fingers deep, a wobbling skin where they meet. You drain it off into a jar.

faults.consequence: In a seaway the water is stirred up into the filter: the engine fires and dies when you need it.
faults.laterNote: a tow if she stops in the wrong place

diy.how: Drain the filter bowl on three separate days, then fit a new primary filter element

yard.how: The yard drains and polishes the tank and changes the filters

atSea.text: When the sea gets up, the engine may cough and die.

faults.name: Water in the fuel tank

spawn.cause: Water has condensed in the fuel tank. It came on over the winter: about {n} cold nights' worth of damp air in a tank left part empty.

reveals.text: Under the diesel a cloudy line of water sits in the bottom of the bowl, grey where it meets the fuel. You drain it off into a jar.

faults.consequence: In a seaway the water is stirred up into the filter: the engine fires and dies when you need it.
faults.laterNote: a tow if she stops in the wrong place

diy.how: Drain the filter bowl on three separate days, then fit a new primary filter element

yard.how: The yard drains and polishes the tank and changes the filters

faults.note: UNVERIFIED (design note 008): that a part-empty tank over a cold winter grows water in the diesel at this rate is not checked against a real boat.

components.name: Fuel shutoff valve
components.description: A brass lever valve on the tank outlet. The lever is stiff but moves the full quarter turn.

components.name: Fuel supply line
components.description: A clear-sleeved fuel hose, slightly yellowed, clamped at both ends. No weeping at the clamps.

components.name: Primary fuel filter / water separator
components.description: A spin-on filter with a glass bowl below. The element is dusty; a date is faintly visible on the casing.

atSea.text: Working hard for hours, the engine may starve and stumble.

faults.name: Primary fuel filter half clogged

reveals.text: You open the drain and look in the bowl: dark diesel, and black sludge clinging to the walls.
An old date is written on the element in marker, so old that the ink has gone brown.

faults.consequence: Fuel starvation when the sea stirs the tank up: she runs rough or stops.

yard.how: The yard changes the fuel filters

components.name: Lift pump
components.description: A small pump on the front of the block with a priming lever. Ticks when the engine turns.

components.name: Secondary fuel filter
components.description: A small blue-grey canister on the front of the engine, clean on the outside, with a single ring of rust at the base.

components.name: Injection pump
components.description: A compact pump with a stamped plate, bolted tight. The tamper seals are intact.

components.name: Injectors
components.description: Two stubby injectors under their return pipes, a little carbon around the clamps.

components.name: Fuel return line
components.description: A thin hose back to the tank, clamped with a worm-drive that has started to rust.

components.name: Raw-water seacock
components.description: A bronze ball valve on a through-hull, green with age, the handle stiff.
components.replaceText: You knock out the old seacock, bed a new through-hull and ball valve, and double-clamp the hose.

atSea.text: The bilge will keep taking water the whole way.

faults.name: Weeping raw-water seacock

reveals.text: There's a damp patch in the bilge under the seacock, rimmed with white salt crust.
Salt crust round the valve stem and a bead of water hanging under it: the seacock is weeping at the stem.

escalation.text: The raw-water seacock has seized: the salt has crusted the stem solid and the handle won't move.

faults.note: UNVERIFIED (decision 6): seizing is driven by frost; rain counts only with the saloon floorboards up. Weep rate 0.05 L/h is also unverified (decision 1).
faults.consequence: It weeps now and will seize; a seized seacock can't be shut if a hose lets go.

yard.how: The yard replaces the seacock and through-hull

atSea.text: You won't be able to shut the cooling water off if something goes wrong.

faults.name: Seized raw-water seacock

reveals.text: You lean on the seacock handle. It doesn't move at all: seized solid in the salt.

faults.consequence: Seized shut: no cooling water, the engine overheats within minutes.

diy.how: Cut out and replace the seacock and through-hull

yard.how: The yard cuts out and replaces the seacock

components.name: Raw-water strainer
components.description: A clear-lidded strainer, a little weed and grit in the basket and a faint tidemark inside the glass.

components.name: Raw-water pump
components.description: A bronze-bodied pump on the front of the engine, a faint salt trail beneath the shaft seal.

atSea.text: The cooling water will be weak the whole way, and the pump body leaks into the bilge.

faults.name: Cracked raw-water pump body

spawn.cause: The raw-water pump body has cracked. It came on after {n} hours of frost with raw water left in the engine.

reveals.text: A crust of white salt and a few dried drips on the engine bay floor, right under the raw-water pump.
A hairline crack runs along the bronze pump body from the inlet flange, a bead of salt water standing in it.
The water at the exhaust comes in weak, uneven spurts.

faults.consequence: The engine runs short of cooling water and the pump body leaks into the bilge whenever she is afloat.
faults.laterNote: a tow home if the engine overheats at sea

yard.how: The yard mechanic fits a new raw-water pump

faults.note: UNVERIFIED (design note 008): that raw water left in the pump over frost cracks the body is a domain claim not yet checked with Amit; the 24 frost hours are a placeholder.

components.name: Raw-water impeller
components.description: A rubber impeller, inside the pump behind a six-screw cover.

atSea.text: Under load for hours the engine will run hot.

faults.name: Tired impeller

reveals.text: With the pump cover off, the vanes have taken a set in a curve and two of them are cracked at the root.
The water at the exhaust comes in weaker spurts than you would like.

faults.consequence: The engine will overheat under load at sea: you'll lose cooling when you need it most.
faults.laterNote: a tow home if it sheds its vanes

yard.how: The yard mechanic fits a new impeller

removablePart.name: raw-water pump cover
removablePart.uncoverText: You undo the six screws and lift off the raw-water pump cover.
removablePart.refitText: You put the pump cover back with a new gasket and do up the six screws.

components.name: Heat exchanger
components.description: A cylindrical exchanger with end caps, a thin white crust along one seam, no drips.

atSea.text: The cooling water will be weak, and the engine will run hot under load.

faults.name: Cracked heat exchanger

spawn.cause: The heat exchanger has split. It came on after {n} hours of frost with raw water left in the engine.

reveals.text: Along the seam of the heat exchanger a split has opened, with coolant weeping out and a green crust drying round it.
The water at the exhaust comes in weaker spurts than you would like.

faults.consequence: Coolant weeps out of the split and the engine runs hot under load.
faults.laterNote: a tow home if the engine overheats at sea

yard.how: The yard mechanic fits a new heat exchanger

faults.note: UNVERIFIED (design note 008): that frost splits the heat exchanger when raw water is left in it is a domain claim not yet checked with Amit; the 48 frost hours are a placeholder.

components.name: Thermostat
components.description: Hidden in its housing, as it should be. The housing gasket is dry and a little brittle.

components.name: Coolant
components.description: Green-pink coolant in the header tank, a shade murkier than it was. Level at the line.

components.name: Exhaust elbow
components.description: A cast elbow where the water meets the exhaust, a rust-brown stain at the lower flange.

components.name: Exhaust hose
components.description: A black wet-exhaust hose looping up under the cockpit, stiff, not cracked, clamps doubled.

atSea.text: The exhaust hose is cooked; the engine room may fill with steam and fumes.

faults.name: Exhaust hose cooked

reveals.text: The hose by the elbow is hard and blistered, the rubber cooked brown: it ran hot and dry.

faults.consequence: It will split and pour exhaust and water into the boat when she runs.

diy.how: Fit a new wet-exhaust hose and clamps

yard.how: The yard fits a new exhaust hose

components.name: Anti-siphon loop
components.description: A vented loop high in the cockpit locker, with a little white salt around the vent.

components.name: Engine block
components.description: A grey Nordvik twin-cylinder, paint worn at the corners, a faint sheen of oil beneath the sump.

components.name: Engine oil
components.description: The dipstick shows oil the colour of tea, within the marks.

components.name: Oil filter
components.description: A blue spin-on canister, rust around the base, a last service sticker curling at the edge.

components.name: Alternator
components.description: A small 60 A alternator on the front bracket, grimy but turning freely by hand.

components.name: Alternator belt
components.description: A narrow V-belt with a glazed shine on the flanks and a small dusting of black on the pulley.

atSea.text: The battery won't be charged while you motor.

faults.name: Slipping alternator belt

reveals.text: You press the belt mid-span: it gives a good inch, and the flanks are glazed. It's slipping on the pulley.

faults.consequence: The battery isn't charging while she runs; it will go flat.

diy.how: Fit a new belt and set the tension

yard.how: The yard fits a new belt

components.name: Glow plugs
components.description: Two glow plugs sunk into the head, thin wires on their caps, a fleck of carbon at each.
components.note: healthyOhms 0.8 is an unverified placeholder, decision 4

components.name: Hull
components.description: Cream gelcoat gone chalky, a few spider cracks at the toerail and a faded waterline stripe.

faults.name: Blistered old paint at the bow

reveals.text: You press a blister at the bow with a thumbnail. It is old paint lifting off older paint, dry and hollow; the gelcoat underneath is hard and sound. Not osmosis.

faults.consequence: Nothing: old paint lifting, the laminate is sound.

components.name: Keel
components.description: A cast-iron keel, rust bleeding from the bolts at the joint, a thin line of filler along the seam.

components.name: Rudder
components.description: A spade rudder with a small bit of play at the bottom, the blade fair and sound.

components.name: Standing rig
components.description: A tall alloy mast, shrouds a little dull, turnbuckles safety-wired in tape that has seen better summers.

components.name: Antifouling
components.description: Red-brown bottom paint, chalky and thin at the waterline, with a few patches of old blue beneath.
components.replaceText: You sand, wipe down and roll on two fresh coats of antifouling.

faults.name: Thin antifouling

reveals.text: The paint is worn through to the old primer along the waterline and on the leading edge of the keel.

faults.consequence: Weed and barnacles by midsummer: a knot slower, and a scrub that needs a lift.
faults.laterNote: afloat: needs a lift and a scrub

diy.how: Sand and roll on two coats of antifouling

yard.how: The yard paints the bottom

components.name: Navigation lights
components.description: A bicolour light on the pulpit and a white stern light, the wiring taped where it runs down the stanchion.
components.replaceText: You fit a new lens on the bicolour light and seal the gasket.

faults.name: Cracked navigation light lens

reveals.text: The bicolour lens has a crack through the red side, and there's a bead of water inside.

faults.consequence: Water gets into the fitting and the bow light fails at night.

yard.how: The yard electrician fits a new lens

components.name: Cockpit drain hoses
components.description: Two reinforced hoses from the cockpit drains down to their through-hulls, each held by a pair of hose clamps.
components.replaceText: You fit new stainless hose clamps, two to each hose tail.

atSea.text: Spray and green water may find their way into the boat.

faults.name: Rusted cockpit drain hose clamps
faults.note: UNVERIFIED (decision 1): 1.5 L of rain in per mm through the rusted clamps.

reveals.text: The clamps are rusted through at the screw housing; one crumbles when you press it with a thumb.

escalation.text: The cockpit drain hose has come off its tail: a rusted clamp let go and the hose slipped off the through-hull.

faults.consequence: A clamp that lets go floods the boat through the drain through-hull.
faults.laterNote: can be done afloat, with the drain seacock shut

yard.how: The yard renews the clamps

atSea.text: Water will come in through the cockpit drain whenever the sea is up.

faults.name: Cockpit drain hose off its tail
faults.note: UNVERIFIED (decision 1): 60 L/h afloat through the open through-hull.

arrivalSign.text: The cockpit drain hose hangs loose from its tail; you can see it through the gap at the cockpit-locker lid. Worth lifting the lid.

reveals.text: The drain hose has slipped right off its through-hull tail and hangs loose; the rusted clamps lie in the bottom of the locker.

faults.consequence: With the hose off, the through-hull is open to the sea and the cockpit no longer drains.
faults.laterNote: can be done afloat, with the drain seacock shut

diy.how: Push the hose back on its tail and fit new doubled clamps

yard.how: The yard refits the drain hose with new clamps

components.name: Lifelines
components.description: Plastic-coated wire lifelines on four stanchions each side, swaged terminals at the pulpit and pushpit.
components.replaceText: You fit new lifeline terminals and tension the wires.

faults.name: Pitted lifeline terminals

reveals.text: Under the plastic the swaged terminals at the pushpit are pitted, rust weeping where the wire goes in.

faults.consequence: A terminal that lets go when someone falls against it.

yard.how: The yard rigger renews the terminals

components.name: Sprayhood
components.description: A navy canvas sprayhood on a stainless frame over the companionway, the clear window gone milky and the zips stiff with salt.
components.replaceText: You fit a new sprayhood on the frame: the canvas laced on, the zips run, the window clear.

faults.name: Torn sprayhood

spawn.cause: The sprayhood has split along its seams. It came on after {n} day{s} of snow lying on it with no cover on her.

reveals.text: The sprayhood sags on its frame, the canvas puckered along the top seams.
The top seams have split along the stitching, rotten where the snow lay on them, and daylight shows through.

faults.consequence: Rain and spray come into the cockpit through the split. It is untidy and wet, and no worse than that.
faults.laterNote: nothing worse; it only gets wetter in the cockpit

yard.how: The sailmaker makes and fits a new sprayhood

faults.note: UNVERIFIED (design note 008): that snow lying on an uncovered sprayhood splits it is a domain claim not yet checked with Amit; the 4 snow days are a placeholder.

components.name: Mooring lines
components.description: Three-strand mooring lines, grey-green with age, spliced eyes over the bow cleats and worn pale where they run through the fairleads.
components.replaceText: You make up a pair of new lines on the bow cleats, with chafe sleeves at the fairleads.

components.name: Bilge
components.description: The lowest part of the hull under the saloon sole, where everything that gets in ends up.

components.name: Bilge pump
components.description: A small submersible pump bolted down at the lowest point of the bilge, a float switch on a short arm beside it. A two-core cable runs aft and up to the battery, through a fuse in a holder by the battery switch.
components.replaceText: You unbolt the old pump, bolt a new one down at the low point, fit the float switch beside it and splice the cable.

atSea.text: The bilge pump will not run, so any water that comes in stays in.

faults.name: Burnt-out bilge pump

reveals.text: The pump body is hot-smelling and the impeller housing is scorched; it hums but nothing moves.

faults.consequence: The bilge has no pump: whatever comes in stays in, and the float switch clicks for nothing.

diy.how: Fit a new pump and float switch

yard.how: The yard fits a new bilge pump

components.name: Anchor and chain
components.description: A plough anchor in the roller at the stem and a length of galvanised chain coiled below it in the chain locker, the zinc long gone from the links.
components.replaceText: You lay out the old chain, shackle on a new length to the anchor and flake it down in the locker.

atSea.text: You can't anchor: the chain would jam in the hawse.

faults.name: Seized anchor chain

reveals.text: The last few metres of chain are rusted solid, the links frozen at odd angles. It would never run out through the gypsy.

faults.consequence: At anchor the chain jams and she won't hold.
faults.laterNote: a night on a borrowed line, and a yard bill all the same

diy.how: Fit a new length of chain

yard.how: The yard fits a new anchor chain

faults.note: UNVERIFIED (design note 010, second pass F): that a 28-footer of this age has chain that seizes, and what a new length costs. Woken only by the escalation of anchor-shackle-frozen.

components.name: Hand-pump heads
components.description: A hand-pump marine toilet bolted to the forepeak sole, the bowl stained, the pump handle stiff, a joker valve in the outlet hose behind the pump.

components.name: Joker valve
components.description: A rubber duckbill valve in the heads' outlet hose, just behind the pump, grey and stiff with age.
components.replaceText: You pinch off the outlet hose, cut the old valve out, push a new joker valve into the hose and clamp it. The forepeak smells of nothing at all by evening.

atSea.text: The heads smell, and will on any passage; nobody will want to use them.

faults.name: Weeping joker valve

reveals.text: A faint smell of sewage hangs in the forepeak, sweetish and stale, strongest by the heads.
A bead of damp at the pump's outlet, and the rubber flap of the joker valve is worn thin and does not seat: it weeps back into the pump.

faults.consequence: The heads smell, and a guest will not use them.

yard.how: The yard fits a new joker valve

faults.note: UNVERIFIED (design note 010, second pass F): that a joker valve of this age weeps, how long one lasts, and what the yard charges for an hour.

components.name: Spirit stove
components.description: An old two-burner alcohol stove in a gimbal by the companionway, the brass burners blackened. It works, but slowly: the kettle takes its time.

components.name: Anchor shackle
components.description: The galvanised shackle that joins the chain to the anchor's eye, its pin furred with rust.
components.replaceText: You knock out the rusted pin with a punch, shackle the chain to the anchor with a new shackle and seize the pin with wire.

atSea.text: The chain will run, but the shackle is rusted solid at the anchor's eye and the whole rode is going the same way.

faults.name: Rusted chain with a frozen shackle

reveals.text: The chain where it leaves the roller is brown with rust.
The shackle pin is rusted into the anchor's eye; the chain is brown with rust but the links still move.

escalation.text: The anchor chain has seized: the rust has locked the links solid in the locker and it will not run.

faults.consequence: Left alone through a wet season the rust works up the chain until it seizes solid.
faults.laterNote: a whole new length of chain, not a shackle

yard.how: The yard fits a new shackle

faults.note: UNVERIFIED (design note 010, second pass F): how fast galvanised chain with no zinc left seizes in a wet season; the rate is rain-weighted exposure with its own spread.

opening: As instructed I surveyed your 28-foot sloop ashore in her cradle at the yard. The hull was sounded and viewed from the ground, the deck and rig from deck level, the machinery as found. The engine was tried. I did not go aloft or strip any machinery.
My findings, in the order I made them:
closing: Items marked Before launch should be attended to before she goes in. The rest can be planned over the season.

items.text: Blistering noted at the bow below the waterline, possibly osmotic. Recommend moisture readings and a closer inspection.
Thin, worn to primer at the waterline and on the keel's leading edge. Recommend a fresh coat before launch.
Weeping at the stem, with salt crust in the bilge below. Recommend service or replacement before launch.
Hose clamps rusted, one failing. Recommend renewal, doubled.
Terminals pitted, rust weeping at the swages aft. Recommend replacement.
Bicolour lens cracked, water inside. Recommend replacement.
No defects visible from deck level. A rigger's inspection aloft is recommended within two seasons.
Dated three seasons back, history unknown. Recommend a load test, and replacement if it does not hold up.
On a trial start the starter clicked once and did not turn the engine. Poor cranking; recommend investigation of the starter circuit.
A sample drawn from the bottom of the tank shows free water. Recommend draining and polishing the tank, and new filters, before launch.
Element marked with a date well past its service interval. Recommend a new element.
Light external rust at the flange, no weeping. Serviceable; monitor.

electrical.name: Connection not done up tight (your own work)
electrical.reveal: Looking again at your own work, the connection moves when you wiggle it: not done up tight.
electrical.consequence: It can work loose under way and leave you without power.

diy.how: Redo it and tighten it properly

yard.how: The yard electrician redoes it

cooling.name: Hose clamp not seated (your own work)

water.soleText: Water stands over the saloon sole.
water.harbourmasterText: The harbourmaster rang: she's sitting low on her mooring. Worth getting down there.

ports.name: Skjærvik
arrivalLines: The mooring buoy comes up out of the grey, and you hook it on the second try.
She swings to the wind, and the yard sheds stand where you left them.
You're home. The engine ticks as it cools.

ports.name: Hestholmen
arrivalLines: Hestholmen opens up round the point: a quay, a few masts, a shop with its door propped open.
A man in a yellow jacket waves you onto a mooring and takes your line without a word.

ports.name: Storholmen
arrivalLines: Storholmen is a low island with a white light on its point and a harbour no bigger than a yard.
A fuel pump on the quay, a kiosk with a tin roof, and a woman who looks up from her crossword just long enough to nod you in.
The wind drops behind the breakwater. The engine ticks as it cools, and you think about how far home is.

ports.name: Kvitnes
arrivalLines: Kvitnes is a bay of white shingle inside a ring of low hills, and nothing built on it but a boathouse with no door.
The anchor finds the sand on the second try, and she swings quietly to it.
Gulls, the slap of water along the hull, and not another boat in sight. It is very still.
arrivalLinesAnchorJammed: Kvitnes is a bay of white shingle inside a ring of low hills, and nothing built on it but a boathouse with no door.
The chain jams after a few metres. You lie to a line on the boathouse ring instead, uneasy all night.
Gulls, the slap of water along the hull, and not another boat in sight. It is very still.

chafeWords.text: The lines are sound: the lay is tight and the eyes are clean at the cleats.
A little fuzz where the lines run through the fairleads, nothing that matters yet.
Strands have rubbed through at the fairleads and the lines are badly chafed. One more blow could finish them.
The lines are chafed almost through, a few strands holding.

events.name: The regatta party at Hestholmen
madeLines: By evening the regatta party has spilled down onto the jetty, lanterns lit, someone playing a fiddle badly and nobody minding.
You sit in the cockpit with a mug and listen. She got you here.
events.missedText: The regatta party at Hestholmen came and went without you.

events.name: Midsummer at Storholmen
madeLines: They light the bonfire on the point at ten, and it burns on into a night that never quite goes dark.

Somebody hands you a plate of herring and a mug of coffee that is mostly something else. Out on the mooring she rides to her line, pale against the water, and the sky over the island stays the colour of milk till morning.
events.missedText: Midsummer came and went, and the bonfire at Storholmen burned without you.

events.name: A friend's week aboard

requires.text: warm enough below on the last night, if it is cold

beats.comeBackLine: You come back for your friend: the ferry is in, and someone is coming down the pontoon.
madeLines: Your friend comes down the pontoon with a rucksack and a bag of oranges, looks round the saloon, and says that it is better than they remembered.

failedLines.heads: Your friend opens the forepeak door, takes one breath, shuts it again, and books the hotel by the ferry.
failedLines.stove: Your friend looks round the galley for something to cook on, says nothing at all, and goes ashore to find something hot to eat.
failedLines.bunk-cushions: Your friend lies down on the saloon berth, sits up again at once, and says the cushions are damp. The week goes home with them.

beats.ask: any day of the week: a passage to Hestholmen with your friend aboard, made in the normal way (a tow does not count)
announceLines: Your friend has looked at the chart and wants to see Hestholmen.
madeLines: Your friend stands in the bow all the way in, pointing at things, and on the quay at Hestholmen buys two ice creams and a postcard of the harbour you are standing in.
beats.missedText: The week goes by without Hestholmen. Your friend is polite about it, and looks at the chart a little longer than necessary.

beats.comeBackLine: You come back for the evening: it is your friend's last night aboard.
beats.morningLine: You come back: it is your friend's last night aboard tonight.
madeLines: The heater ticks and glows below, and your friend sits in the warm with a mug and says it is the best last night of any holiday.
passLines: The last night is mild enough to sit out in the cockpit till late, and nobody thinks about the heater at all.

failedLines.diesel-heater: By the last evening your friend is in two jumpers and a hat, below, and asks gently whether there is heating. There is not.

beats.missedText: The last night finds her at sea, and your friend's farewell supper is a sandwich at the chart table.

good.line: A good week: the island trip and the last night both came off, and your friend goes home talking about it.
good.short: a good week: the day trip and the last night

made.line: A week, and one of the two things your friend wanted came off.
made.short: a week: one of the day trip and the last night

thin.line: A thin week: your friend came aboard, and the island trip and the last night came to nothing.
thin.short: a thin week: neither the day trip nor the last night

events.walkLine: Your friend goes walking on the island while you are at work.
events.inviteCostLine: Weekdays you spend with your friend cost vacation days as usual.
events.missedText: Your friend waited on the quay at Skjærvik and took the evening ferry home.

events.name: The club cruise to Kvitnes

lines: You come in on the Friday evening as the raft is forming: the club skipper waves you into the line with a boat hook, and you spend the first night in the middle of it, hearing the whole bay settle.
early.log: She made the Friday evening raft-up at Kvitnes.

madeLines: Eleven boats lie to their anchors in the bay at Kvitnes, and by dusk a raft of dinghies has gathered round the biggest one.
Someone passes a thermos down the line. Nobody here owns a shop or a fuel pump, and nobody needs one tonight.

failedLines.anchor-gear: The club lies in a ring round the bay, each boat to its own anchor, and you on a borrowed line among them. Nobody says anything. Everybody knows.
failedLines.bilge-pump: The club skipper looks over your rail at the bilge, and at the pump that hums and moves nothing, and asks politely whether you mean to stay.

events.missedText: The club cruise to Kvitnes went without you.

closeCalls.letterBillText: The harbourmaster's letter: the cost of a ferry's report.
closeCalls.letterAlert: A letter from the harbourmaster's office: the ferry {ferry} reported you at about {hour} on day {day}. It bills {nok}, and the letter is in the logbook.

narrations.text: A ferry's horn, close and getting closer; then her wake slaps the hull and she is gone into the grey.
A wall of white steel slides past a boat length off, a man on her bridge wing looking down at you. Her wash rolls the boat for a minute after.
A rock you never saw goes past close enough to touch, white water round it.
A moored fishing float comes out of the grey dead ahead. You put the helm over and it scrapes down the side.

fog.reportLine: She was a ferry, and her master will have written you into his log: the harbour will hear of it.

narrations.text: A searchlight comes swinging across the water from a ferry's bridge and stops on you. You put a hand up against the glare. Her horn gives one long blast, and she slides past close enough to read her name.
A wall of lit windows is suddenly there, a ferry you never saw, her bow wave already lifting you. A man on her bridge wing looks down at your dark boat.
A fishing boat's bow comes out of the dark with its deck lamps glaring, and swings away a boat length off. Her wash slaps the hull, and a man shouts something you cannot make out.
Something low and black is dead ahead: a fishing boat at her nets, and you saw no light until you were on her. You put the helm hard over and her warp scrapes down the side.

night.reportLine: She was a ferry, and her master will have called you in: the harbour will hear of it.
night.letterText: Dear owner, the ferry {ferry} reported an unlit sailing boat in the fairway at about {hour} on day {day}, her sail number matching yours. A boat under way after dark shows her navigation lights. The harbour keeps every such report on file and bills the cost of answering it, {nok}. Please have her lights seen to before you sail after dark again. Yours, the harbourmaster's office.
night.planLine: without them a ferry may not see her, and ferries report.

radio.noSign: You give the boat's name; there is no call sign to give.
radio.unheard: You call three times. The set hisses with other boats' traffic: you can hear them; nobody hears you.
radio.reportedNote: The coast radio logs every call, and one made with no call sign will be reported: the harbour will hear of it.

lines: there's room on the guest pontoon.
the guest pontoon is full, but the end of the fuel quay is free for an hour.
the pontoon is yours for the night; the water is on, the showers are shut.
ask for the harbourmaster's mooring, the second buoy from the breakwater.
harbour.noOffice: You call three times. Nobody answers: {port} is an anchorage, with no harbour office to listen.

coast.call: You call on channel {channel}: 'Coast radio, coast radio, coast radio, {identity}. Over.'
coast.answer: Coast radio answers: '{boat}, coast radio. Go to channel {working}.' On {working}, you ask for a radio check. 'Loud and clear. I read you strength five. Over.' You say: 'Thank you, {boat}. Out.'
coast.forecast: Then the coast radio reads the forecast. {forecast}

ferry.call: Channel 16: 'Sailing yacht {where}, this is the ferry {ferry}, {ferry}, {ferry}. Do you read? Over.' The set on the chart table is calling you.
ferry.answer: You lift the handset and answer: '{ferry}, {ferry}, {ferry}, {identity}. I read you. Over.' 'Sailing yacht {boat}, {ferry}. I have you. I will pass astern of you. Out.' She passes astern, close, her wash rolling you for a minute, and no horn.
ferry.nobody: Nobody is calling you; the ferries are working their own channels.
ferry.waiting: The ferry {ferry} is calling you on channel 16.
ferry.log: Spoke to the ferry {ferry} on channel 16; she passed astern.

letter.billText: The harbourmaster's letter: a radio call made without a ticket.
letter.alert: A letter from the harbourmaster's office: the coast radio logged a call from your boat at about {time} on day {day}, made with no call sign. It bills {nok}, and the letter is in the logbook.
letter.text: Dear owner, the coast radio logged a call from a sailing boat of your name and number at about {time} on day {day}, made on channel {channel} with no call sign. A radio may be used only by the holder of an operator's certificate, and the station reports every call that is not. The harbour keeps every such report on file and bills the cost of answering it, {nok}. Please do not call again until you hold the radio ticket. Yours, the harbourmaster's office.

words.text: The yard has started asking for payment before the work.
The yard is polite with you, and a little careful.
The yard knows your boat, not yet you.
The yard knows you pay on time.
The yard keeps an eye on her for you, and the towboat skipper waves.

component.name: Diesel heater
component.description: A small diesel bulkhead heater under the quarter berth, its flue run up through the deck and its fuel line tee'd into the tank.
component.replaceText: You take the old heater off the bulkhead and fit a new one on the same flue.

upgrades.opens: the friend's week in a cold July
upgrades.installText: You cut the flue through the deck, seal it, bolt the heater to the bulkhead and tee its fuel line into the tank feed. You light it once to burn off the oil, and the saloon smells of hot paint for an hour.

component.name: Marine heads with holding tank
component.description: A marine toilet bolted to the forepeak sole, its outlet piped to a holding tank under the V-berth, with its seacock and hoses.
component.replaceText: You pull the old heads and fit a new pump on the same hoses.

upgrades.opens: a heads that does not smell, for the friend's week
upgrades.installText: You unbolt the old hand-pump heads and carry it up through the hatch, valve and all, then bolt the new heads to the sole, set the holding tank under the V-berth, fit the hoses and pump it through twice with the seacocks open. It works, and nothing leaks, and nothing smells.

component.name: Gas stove
component.description: A gimballed gas stove with two burners and an oven by the companionway, on its own gas bottle with a shut-off at the locker.
component.replaceText: You swap the old stove for a new one on the same gas hose.

upgrades.opens: a quick kettle, and an oven
upgrades.installText: You lift the old spirit stove out of its gimbal and fit the gas stove in the galley recess, gimbals on their pins, the gas hose run to the locker and tested with soapy water.

component.name: Chart plotter
component.description: A small chart plotter on a bracket by the companion hatch, wired to the nav panel with an inline fuse; its power lead plugs into a socket behind the binnacle.
component.replaceText: You swap the plotter on its bracket and re-key the boat's details.

faults.name: Corroded plotter plug
faults.symptom: The plotter screen has gone blank; it comes back when you jiggle the plug behind the binnacle, then goes again.

atSea.text: The plotter screen goes blank whenever it rains, so on a wet day it is no plotter at all; on a dry day it works.

spawn.cause: The plotter's power plug has corroded. It came on from the cockpit rain and the spray at sea that reach the socket behind the binnacle.

reveals.text: The pins of the power plug behind the binnacle are furred with green corrosion, and the socket is damp.
You pull the plug, scrape the green off the pins with a small screwdriver and spray them with contact cleaner.

faults.consequence: The plotter blanks in the rain, which is just when you want it, and works on a dry day, which is when you don't need it.
faults.laterNote: nothing worse; the screen only blanks more often

diy.how: Clean the plug's pins and refit it

yard.how: The yard cleans the plug and puts a dab of grease on the pins

faults.note: UNVERIFIED (design note 010, second pass G): how fast an unsealed plug in a cockpit corrodes in rain and spray, and that it blanks the screen only when wet. Cleaning is the fix because a new plotter for a dirty plug would be absurd; it can corrode again.

upgrades.opens: leaving the harbour in fog; 3.5 knots in fog instead of 2
upgrades.installText: You bolt the bracket to the cockpit coaming, run the power lead to the panel with its own fuse and key in the boat's details. The screen comes up blue with the coast drawn on it, and a small boat where you are.

component.name: Marine radar
component.description: A small radome on the mast above the spreaders, the cable run down the outside of the mast to a display at the companionway.
component.replaceText: You lower the old radome and fit a new one on the same bracket.

also.name: Scanner cable
also.description: The radar's cable where it runs down the mast, taped to the spar with a loop at each spreader.
also.replaceText: You go up the mast on a halyard, cut out the old cable run, lead a new one down from the radome and tape it to the spar with a drip loop at the spreader.

faults.name: Chafed scanner cable
faults.symptom: The radar sweeps, but the screen stays empty: not even the shore paints.

atSea.text: The radar paints nothing: it is no help in fog.

spawn.cause: The scanner cable has chafed through where it passes the spreader. It came on from the mast working in the wind, most of all under way.

reveals.text: Where the cable runs past the spreader the outer sheath is worn through and the braid shows, shiny from rubbing on the spar.

faults.consequence: The radar paints nothing, so in fog she is no better off than without it.
faults.laterNote: nothing worse; the radar stays blind until the cable is renewed

diy.how: Run a new scanner cable down the mast

yard.how: The yard runs a new scanner cable

faults.note: UNVERIFIED (design note 010, second pass G): how fast a radar cable chafes where it passes a spreader, how much faster under way than at the mooring, and what a cable run costs.

upgrades.installText: You go up the mast on a halyard with the bracket and the radome, bolt it on above the spreaders and tape the cable down the mast. Below, the display sweeps round and shows the pontoon, the boats beside her and the shore.

component.name: VHF radio
component.description: A fixed VHF set on a bracket at the chart table, with its handset on a coiled lead and a coaxial cable run up the mast to an antenna at the masthead.
component.replaceText: You swap the set on its bracket and plug the handset and the coax into the new one.

also.name: VHF antenna connector
also.description: The coax connector where the VHF cable meets the antenna at the masthead, taped against the weather; from the deck you can look up and see the base of the whip.
also.replaceText: You go up the mast in the bosun's chair with the new connector, cut off the old one, solder the new plug on, tape it and seal it with self-amalgamating tape, and come down again.

faults.name: Corroded VHF antenna connector

spawn.cause: The antenna connector at the masthead has corroded. Rain and spray at sea got in at the plug, and the green has eaten the contact: the set can receive but nothing gets out.

reveals.text: At the base of the antenna the connector is furred with green corrosion, and the tape round it has split.

faults.consequence: The VHF receives but cannot be heard: no call you make is answered, and a ferry that calls you will not hear your answer.
faults.laterNote: nothing worse; the set stays deaf-mute until the connector is renewed

atSea.text: The VHF receives but cannot be heard: no call you make is answered, and a ferry that calls you will not hear your answer.

diy.how: Go up the mast and fit a new antenna connector

yard.how: The yard sends a man up the mast to fit a new antenna connector

faults.note: UNVERIFIED (design note 012, step 3): how fast a masthead antenna connector corrodes in rain and spray, and the price of a connector and an hour aloft. Practice: water intrusion at the connector is a leading cause of marine VHF failure, and a corroded connector often lets the set receive while transmitting badly (Raymarine, West Marine and Simrad notes, sailing forums); the fix is a new connector, sealed.

upgrades.opens: calls on channel 16; the coast radio's forecast; with the radio ticket, a ferry's call in fog or the dark
upgrades.installText: You bolt the set to the bracket at the chart table, run the power lead to the panel with its own fuse, plug the coax in and hang the handset on its hook. The set hisses, then a voice somewhere reads out a position. You are on the air, or would be if you were allowed to be.

component.name: Bunk cushions
component.description: A set of foam cushions for the saloon berths, in washable covers.
component.replaceText: You lay a new set of cushions on the berths.

upgrades.installText: You lay the new cushions along the saloon berths and tuck the covers in. They smell of new foam, and are dry.

component.name: Cockpit varnish
component.description: The teak of the cockpit coamings and seats, sanded and varnished.
component.replaceText: You sand the cockpit back and put on a new coat of varnish.

upgrades.opens: value only: the broker likes bright teak
upgrades.installText: You sand the coamings and seats back to pale wood, wipe them down and put on coat after coat while the weather holds. By evening the cockpit shines and nobody is to sit on it.
